title: Building My Endgame Keyboard (Lubing Switches Is a Trap)
creator: clackbyte
description:
Full build of my new 75% board: gasket mount, lubed linears, tape mod, and a lot of regret about the stabilizers.

Parts:
Case: aluminium 75%, gasket mount
Switches: linears, 63.5g
Keycaps: cherry profile PBT

Sound test at the end.

sentences.t: Okay, today's the day, I'm finally building the keyboard I've been collecting parts for since the summer.
It's a seventy five percent layout, gasket mount, aluminium case, and I've been waiting on the keycaps for four months.
Let's open the case first.
This is heavy, like genuinely heavy, I think it's about two kilos fully built.
Inside you've got the plate, the PCB, and these little silicone gaskets that sit between the plate and the case.
The gaskets are what give it that soft, bouncy typing feel instead of slamming into solid metal.
So first job, stabilizers, and I'm going to be honest, this is the part I hate.
Stabilizers are what keep the long keys like the space bar from wobbling, and if they're not tuned, they rattle.
I'm clipping the little feet, adding some dielectric grease on the wire, and a bit of thicker lube on the housings.
Listen to this one before, that's the rattle, and now after.
Silence, beautiful.
Okay, that was one, and there are four more, so I'll speed this up.
By the way, part of today's video is sponsored by Tidewell.
Now the switches, and this is where I need to warn you about something.
Lubing switches is a trap.
It does make them smoother and quieter, but you have to open every single switch, brush lube on the stem and the housing, and close it again.
I have ninety switches.
I did this over four evenings, and by the end I was dreaming about tiny springs.
Is it worth it?
For linears, yeah, you can really feel the difference, but if anyone tells you it's relaxing, they're lying.
Okay, next, the tape mod.
I'm putting two layers of painter's tape on the back of the PCB, which sounds silly, but it makes the sound deeper and more poppy.
And now into the plate, switches clicking in one by one.
This is the satisfying part, honestly, it's like a really expensive Lego set.
Plate goes onto the PCB, everything lines up, and I'm going to plug it in and test every key before I close the case.
Every key works, which never happens on my first try.
Last time I built one of these, the whole bottom row was dead and I had to reflow three solder joints.
So I'm going to take this as a sign from the universe.
Case goes back together, eight screws, and now the keycaps.
These are cherry profile, PBT plastic, with this cream and navy colour scheme that I love.
And there it is.
I'm really happy with how this looks, the colours match the desk perfectly.
Okay, sound test, I'm going to type a paragraph and then do some fast space bar spam.
That's deep, that's exactly the sound I wanted, that thocky marble sound.
Now, would I recommend this to a beginner?
Not this exact build, it's a lot of work and a lot of money.
Start with something hot-swappable, where you can change switches without soldering, and work up from there.
Let me know what you think of the sound in the comments.
